## Where we are

- Deck 04: selection leaves **local** marks on diversity against a genome-wide background.
- Plants are rooted — they can't flee a stress — so they **adapt in place** to soils,
  climate, and elevation, often over remarkably short distances.
- **Today:** the theory of **migration–selection balance**, and how we **find** the loci
  behind local adaptation. *(Computer Activity 2 follows; sets up the Sep 17 GEA discussion.)*

## Learning objectives

By the end you should be able to:

- Write the one-locus fitness scheme and the direction of allele-frequency change.
- Derive when **selection beats migration** to maintain a locally adaptive allele.
- Interpret **clines** along environmental gradients.
- Outline how **$F_{ST}$ outliers** and **GEA** detect adaptive loci, and their pitfalls.

# Selection in one population {.center}

## One-locus directional selection (recap)

Relative fitnesses for a favored allele $A_1$ (selection coefficient $s$, dominance $h$):

$$
\begin{array}{c|ccc}
\text{genotype} & A_1A_1 & A_1A_2 & A_2A_2 \\ \hline
w & 1 & 1 - sh & 1 - s
\end{array}
$$

The per-generation change in the favored allele:

$$
\Delta p = \frac{p q\,\big[\,p(w_{11}-w_{12}) + q(w_{12}-w_{22})\,\big]}{\bar w} .
$$

- Selection pushes $p$ deterministically; **drift** (deck 01) and **migration** (next)
  oppose it.

# Migration–selection balance {.center}

## A two-population model

Two demes, opposite alleles favored (haploid, selection $s$), with a fraction $m$ of each
deme replaced by migrants from the other each generation (Coop, Ch 11):

$$
\begin{array}{c|cc}
 & \text{allele } 1 & \text{allele } 2 \\ \hline
\text{pop 1} & 1 & 1 - s \\
\text{pop 2} & 1 - s & 1
\end{array}
$$

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
- **Selection** ($\Delta_S \approx s\,p q$) pulls each deme toward its *local* allele.
- **Migration** ($\Delta_M \approx -m\,(p - \bar p)$) pulls both toward the *average*.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

favored, migrants $m$ exchanged each generation.

## When does local adaptation persist?

Balancing the two forces, a locally adaptive polymorphism is maintained only when
selection outpaces gene flow:

$$
\boxed{\,s > m\,}\qquad\text{(otherwise migration swamps local adaptation).}
$$

- Below threshold ($m > s$): the immigrant allele **swamps** the deme; local adaptation
  collapses.
- The frequency of the locally **maladaptive** immigrant allele sits near $\sim m/s$.

::: {.callout-note}
Same algebra as mutation–selection balance (deck-04 toolbox), with **migration** rather
than **mutation** as the source of maladaptive alleles.
:::

## Clines and a classic plant example

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="52%"}
- A **cline** is a gradient of allele frequency across an environmental transition; its
  **width** scales with $\sigma/\sqrt{s}$ (dispersal vs. selection).
- ***Anthoxanthum odoratum*** at mine boundaries: **zinc tolerance** flips over **meters**
  across the mine edge, despite pollen and seed flow — selection is that strong
  [@antonovics1971].
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}

# Finding the loci {.center}

## Method I — $F_{ST}$ outlier scans

- Local adaptation **inflates $F_{ST}$** at the responsible loci above the genome-wide
  (demographic) background — the deck-02/04 outlier logic.
- Flag loci in the upper tail of the genome-wide $F_{ST}$ distribution.

::: {.callout-important}
**Confounds:** neutral structure, range expansion, and **background selection** all create
$F_{ST}$ outliers. A credible scan needs a **demographic null**, not a naïve quantile cutoff.
:::

::: {.figure-prompt}
**FIGURE** — Manhattan plot of $F_{ST}$ with an environmental-variable track aligned
beneath, an outlier peak coinciding with a soil/climate gradient.
:::

<!-- ALT TEXT (required when the image is added) — pick & refine one,
     then set as fig-alt="…" on the ![](…) you insert:
  A) "Genome-wide F_ST scan with an outlier peak that lines up with a mapped environmental gradient track below it."
  B) "Manhattan plot highlighting a differentiation outlier associated with an environmental variable."
-->

## Method II — genotype–environment association (GEA)

Regress allele frequency directly on an environmental variable $E$, **correcting for
population structure** so shared history doesn't masquerade as adaptation:

$$
\mathrm{logit}\,p_\ell = \beta_0 + \beta_1 E + (\text{structure / random effect}) .
$$

- $\beta_1 \neq 0$ ⟹ the locus tracks the environment beyond what structure explains.
- Common tools (**conceptual** here): **LFMM**, **RDA**, **BayPass**.

::: {.notes}
The hard part is always the structure correction: latitude correlates with both climate
and ancestry, so without it you recover demography, not adaptation. This is the crux of the
Sep 17 discussion paper (Dauphin et al. 2020).
:::

## Plants are the model systems here

- ***Arabidopsis thaliana*** — climate-associated alleles across its Eurasian range,
  validated in common gardens.
- **Conifers** (e.g. lodgepole pine, spruce) — GEA for cold/drought adaptation across steep
  elevational gradients.
- *Mimulus*, *Helianthus*, *Boechera* — repeated edaphic and climatic ecotypes.

::: {.callout-tip}
A recurring theme: the **same** environmental challenge often recruits the **same genes**
across lineages — convergence at the molecular level.
:::

<span class="xref">→ Sep 17 discussion: Dauphin et al. (2020), a GEA case study.</span>

# Computer Activity 2 — demystifying the sliding window {.center}

## Simulate two populations with a selected locus

Genome scans (deck 02, and the $F_{ST}$/Tajima panels above) all reduce to **statistics in
windows along the genome**. Let's build one from a coalescent simulation and see the
outlier appear.

```python
import msprime
# Two demes that split, with low ongoing migration
demog = msprime.Demography()
demog.add_population(name="A", initial_size=5000)
demog.add_population(name="B", initial_size=5000)
demog.add_population(name="ANC", initial_size=10000)
demog.add_population_split(time=2000, derived=["A", "B"], ancestral="ANC")
demog.set_migration_rate("A", "B", 1e-4); demog.set_migration_rate("B", "A", 1e-4)

ts = msprime.sim_ancestry(samples={"A": 30, "B": 30}, demography=demog,
                          sequence_length=2e6, recombination_rate=1e-8, random_seed=7)
ts = msprime.sim_mutations(ts, rate=1e-8, random_seed=7)
```

::: {.notes}
Display-only; change ```` ```python ```` to ```` ```{python} ```` and `pip install msprime`
to run live. A neutral simulation has no true sweep — the exercise is to (a) see the null
window distribution, then (b) inject diversity loss in one region (e.g. trim trees / lower
local diversity) to create an outlier and rediscover it.
:::

## Compute the statistics in windows

```python
import numpy as np
windows = np.linspace(0, ts.sequence_length, 101)   # 100 windows of 20 kb
A = ts.samples(population=0); B = ts.samples(population=1)

fst   = ts.Fst([A, B], windows=windows)             # differentiation per window
tajD_A = ts.Tajimas_D([A], windows=windows)         # within-pop A
```

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
**The point of the activity:**

- A **window too small** is noisy; **too large** smooths the signal away — choose
  deliberately.
- Under neutrality, outliers still appear by **chance** — you need the genome-wide
  distribution as a null.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.figure-prompt}
**FIGURE** — Manhattan plot of windowed $F_{ST}$ (and a Tajima's $D$ track) along the
simulated chromosome, with the planted outlier window highlighted.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
"Demystifying the sliding window": the scan is just **a statistic + a window size + a null**.
Every choice changes which peaks you call. <span class="xref">→ same logic powers the GEA and
$F_{ST}$ scans above.</span>
:::

## Summary

$$
\Delta p = \frac{pq[\,p(w_{11}-w_{12})+q(w_{12}-w_{22})\,]}{\bar w}
\qquad
\text{local adaptation persists iff } s > m
$$

- Local adaptation is a tug-of-war: **selection** builds it, **gene flow** erodes it.
- **Clines** are its geographic signature; width $\sim \sigma/\sqrt{s}$.
- **$F_{ST}$ outliers** and **GEA** find the loci — both demand a **structure/demography
  control** to avoid false positives.
